analysis.one_liner: Bars giant digital ad companies like Google from owning both sides of the ad market, and requires ad brokers to serve their customers' best interests.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: it sat in the Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee from May 2022 until Congress ended in January 2023, despite four cosponsors split evenly between the two parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written new rules into antitrust law for companies that buy and sell digital ads on behalf of others. Companies with more than $20 billion in annual digital ad revenue — chiefly Google, and potentially Amazon and Meta — could no longer own the ad marketplace, the software that helps advertisers buy ads, and the software that helps publishers sell ads all at the same time. Companies with more than $5 billion in ad revenue acting as brokers would have a legal duty to act in their customers' best interest and get the best available price, similar to the duty financial advisers owe, plus public reports on how ads were routed and priced. Enforcement would come from the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits [S2][S3]. The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on May 19, 2022, then to its antitrust subcommittee on November 1, 2022, and it never advanced further [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that buy ads and websites that sell ad space — including small advertisers and news publishers — who today hand a large share of their ad budgets to middlemen they cannot see into. If competition improves, the cost of ads embedded in the prices of goods and services could also fall for consumers. Under the bill, brokerage customers could sue and recover the greater of $1,000 per month of violation or actual damages, with attorney's fees [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill stops any company with more than $20 billion in digital advertising revenue from owning an ad exchange and a buy-side or sell-side brokerage, or owning a brokerage while also trading ads for itself — the core conflict of interest in today's market [S3].

It requires brokers with more than $5 billion in ad revenue to act in their customers' best interest and seek the most favorable terms available for each order, mirroring fiduciary duties in financial markets [S2][S3].
It gives advertisers and publishers the right to request the bids received, winning prices, routing practices, and compensation paid — information that today is almost entirely hidden from them [S3].

Brokerage customers get a private right of action with damages of the greater of $1,000 per month of violation or actual harms, plus a ban on class-action waivers, and enforcement by the Justice Department and state attorneys general [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest digital ad platforms — Google above all, which the CRS summary names as the prime example of a company that owns both an exchange and publisher software — plus any other firm above the $20 billion threshold. They would have to divest parts of their ad businesses within a year and comply with transparency, privacy, and certification rules. Firms above $5 billion would face compliance costs for fiduciary and reporting duties [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Google and other giant ad platforms

drawbacks.text: Divestiture is disruptive: the tooling that millions of advertisers and publishers use today is integrated, and forcing a company like Google to sell or spin off parts of it within a one-year effective window could temporarily disrupt services that small businesses rely on [S3].

The fiduciary, reporting, and time-synchronization requirements impose real compliance costs on any firm above $5 billion in ad revenue, and the government had no experience supervising ad markets the way it does securities markets, so enforcement would need to be built from scratch [S3].

Critics of mandated structural separation generally argue that integration can produce efficiencies that lower costs, and that courts and the Justice Department, rather than statutory bans, are better positioned to weigh those trade-offs case by case; the bill chooses bright-line separation instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a market where studies widely cited in antitrust circles estimate a large fraction of every advertising dollar never reaches a publisher — but those estimates are not in the provided sources, so this analysis relies on the bill's own structure. The structural fix is simple and targeted: fewer than a handful of companies exceed the $20 billion threshold. The costs — one-time divestitures and ongoing compliance — fall on a few firms with enormous margins; the gains go to the millions of businesses and publishers on the other side of the market and, potentially, to consumers through lower prices. The main honest objection is transition risk and the difficulty of building a new regulatory regime; those are manageable design questions rather than reasons the market would be worse off. On balance the benefits outweigh the costs for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Judiciary Committee in May 2022 and to its antitrust subcommittee in November 2022, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Buck introduced the bill on May 19, 2022 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
The cosponsor list reached four members, split evenly between two Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
On November 1, 2022, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large ad platforms that dominate digital advertising — Google above all — are better off, because the bill that would have forced them to separate their ad businesses died in committee without ever coming to a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Google and the giant ad platforms

for.name: Ken Buck
for.role: Chair of the House Antitrust Subcommittee's ranking member bloc; sponsor of H.R. 7839 (he was Ranking Member of the Judiciary Antitrust Subcommittee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 19, 2022, framing it as preventing conflicts of interest in digital advertising

for.name: David Cicilline
for.role: Representative (RI-01) and Chair of the House Judiciary Antitrust Subcommittee

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (party leadership-D during the 117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the remainder of the Congress without holding a markup or vote, instead referring it to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022

against.name: Google
against.role: Largest operator of both digital ad exchanges and buy- and sell-side software; named in the CRS summary as the bill's example target
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed forced structural separation of its advertising business and lobbied against ad-tech break-up legislation

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four cosponsors split evenly — two Republicans and two Democrats — and it died in committee without any roll call that would have shown how the chambers would have divided.

industries.industry: Google and other giant digital ad platforms (over $20 billion in ad revenue)
industries.note: They would have had to divest either their ad exchange or their buy- and sell-side brokerage software, ending the arrangement in which the same firm runs the marketplace, advises both sides of each deal, and trades for itself. Advertisers and publishers pay the resulting conflict-of-interest costs through higher ad prices and lower publisher payouts.

industries.industry: Digital ad brokers above $5 billion in ad revenue
industries.note: Those large enough to be exempt from divestiture would still owe a best-interest duty, best-execution duty, quarterly public routing reports, and annual certification to the Attorney General — meaning oversight costs in exchange for staying in business.

industries.industry: Advertisers and digital publishers, including news media
industries.note: They gain enforceable transparency rights, data ownership of their own bids, and a private right of action with damages of at least $1,000 per month of violation; any savings in ad middlemen costs also flow toward consumer prices.
